analysis.one_liner: Grants college athletes the right to unionize and bargain collectively with their schools and conferences.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in December 2023, referred to the Senate labor committee, and never received a hearing, a vote, or floor action before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the National Labor Relations Act so that college athletes who receive scholarships or other pay tied to playing a sport count as employees. It would let them form unions and bargain collectively with their colleges and athletic conferences over pay, working conditions, and health and safety—including multi-school bargaining units across an entire conference. It also bars athletes from being forced to sign away these rights, and specifies that compensation would not trigger new taxes or jeopardize federal student aid eligibility.
analysis.who_benefits: College athletes who receive scholarships or any compensation tied to playing a sport would gain the legal right to organize and negotiate as a group over compensation, schedules, health and safety protections, and the terms the NCAA and member schools currently set unilaterally. The bill's own findings argue athletes perform services under grant-in-aid agreements that control how and when they work [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Defines any college athlete who receives direct compensation, including grant-in-aid scholarships, as an employee under the National Labor Relations Act, giving them the right to unionize and bargain collectively [S2].
Extends the Act to public institutions of higher education for college athletes, so athletes at state schools are covered even though the NLRA normally does not reach public employers [S2].

Allows bargaining units spanning multiple schools within an athletic conference, with the athlete representatives' consent, so athletes can negotiate league-wide rules rather than school-by-school [S2].
Prohibits athletes from being required to waive these rights in grant-in-aid agreements or legal settlements [S2].
Ensures that compensation received under these arrangements does not become newly taxable or affect eligibility for federal financial aid, addressing a practical concern for athlete-employees [S2].

analysis.who_pays: The NCAA and its member institutions, especially the athletic departments of large revenue-generating programs, would bear the cost of bargaining with athlete unions over compensation and working conditions that they currently control unilaterally. The bill's findings state that intercollegiate sports generate more than $15 billion a year in interstate commerce and that the NCAA and its members have colluded to cap athlete compensation [S2].

drawbacks.text: Opponents of athlete unionization have long argued that treating student-athletes as employees could blur or break the traditional relationship between athletes and their schools; the bill deliberately rejects that framing by classifying any athlete receiving compensation as an employee, which would fundamentally restructure college sports governance [S2].

The bill extends federal labor law to public universities for college athletes, expanding federal jurisdiction over state institutions—a constitutional and federalism objection that the bill itself anticipates by including a severability clause in case parts are struck down [S2].

Multi-conference bargaining units would concentrate negotiating power across rival schools, which could raise costs for athletic departments and force difficult tradeoffs at programs where football and basketball revenue subsidizes other sports; the bill does not address how those schools would absorb the expense [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For athletes, the gains are substantial: enforceable group bargaining over pay, health, and safety instead of unilateral rules set by schools and the NCAA. The costs fall on the college sports enterprise, which would lose its ability to cap athlete compensation and would have to negotiate. The bill is fairly carefully designed—preserving scholarship tax treatment and aid eligibility and allowing (not mandating) conference-wide bargaining—but its broad redefinition of employment would create genuinely hard questions for athletic departments and non-revenue sports. It never got to the point where those tradeoffs were tested: it received no hearing or vote.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate committee that handles labor law, but the committee never held a hearing or vote on it, and it never reached the Senate floor before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Chris Murphy introduced the College Athlete Right to Organize Act on December 6, 2023, joined by Sens. Bernie Sanders and Elizabeth Warren [S2].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions [S4].
Two senators—Bernie Sanders (D-VT) and Elizabeth Warren (D-MA)—cosponsored the bill [S3].
The bill's complete action history ends with that referral: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action were ever recorded before the 118th Congress ended [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The NCAA and its member institutions are better off because the bill never advanced: they keep their current authority to set compensation rules and working conditions for college athletes without having to bargain with athlete unions. The bill's findings describe exactly this status quo—capped compensation and unilateral control over athletes' terms of labor—as the arrangement the bill would have ended [S2].

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The NCAA and its member schools

for.name: Sen. Christopher Murphy
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate.

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral without scheduling a hearing, a markup, or a committee vote for the remainder of the Congress.

against.name: NCAA and member institutions
against.role: Governing body of college sports and its member schools
against.what_they_did: The bill targets their practice of capping athlete compensation and controlling the terms of athletes' participation; they had a direct stake in the bill not becoming law.

sides.party_line_note: All three supporters—Sens. Murphy, Sanders, and Warren—are Democrats or allied independents; no Republican cosponsored the bill, and it received no committee or floor action where votes would have been recorded [S2, S3, S4].

industries.industry: NCAA and member college athletic programs
industries.note: The bill would strip the NCAA and its member schools of unilateral control over athlete compensation and conditions, subjecting them to collective bargaining under federal labor law. The bill's findings describe their current model as capping athlete pay and controlling the terms of athletes' labor in a market generating over $15 billion a year [S2].

Conferences set rules and standards across member schools and would become direct bargaining counterparts to athlete unions, including potential multiemployer bargaining units spanning their member schools [S2].
